title: Functional Programming: List, Dict, and Set Comprehensions

slides.title: Comprehensions Overview
slides.prompt: Comprehensions provide a concise way to create lists, dictionaries, and sets from existing iterables without using explicit for-loops. They support conditional filtering and value transformations.

slides.title: List Comprehension Syntax
slides.prompt: Fill in the correct brackets used to construct a list comprehension.
slides.codeSnippet: evens = ___x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0___

slides.title: Filtering in Comprehensions
slides.prompt: Where should a single 'if' condition filter be placed inside a standard list comprehension?
options: At the end of the comprehension statement (e.g., [x for x in data if condition])
At the very beginning before the expression
Inside an explicit lambda wrapper function
slides.correctAnswer: At the end of the comprehension statement (e.g., [x for x in data if condition])

slides.title: Dictionary Comprehension Syntax
slides.prompt: Fill in the syntax pattern used to map key-value pairs inside a dictionary comprehension.
slides.codeSnippet:
scores = {"Alice": 90, "Bob": 75}
passed = {k___ v for k, v in scores.items() if v >= 80}

slides.title: Ternary Operator in List Comprehension
slides.prompt: How do you write an 'if-else' conditional transformation inside a list comprehension?
options: [val1 if condition else val2 for item in iterable]
[for item in iterable if condition val1 else val2]
[val1 for item in iterable if condition else val2]
[if condition val1 else val2 for item in iterable]
slides.correctAnswer: [val1 if condition else val2 for item in iterable]

slides.title: Set Comprehension Feature
slides.prompt: Fill in the bracket type used to create a Set Comprehension which automatically eliminates duplicate values.
slides.codeSnippet:
words = ["cat", "dog", "cat"]
unique_words = ___w.upper() for w in words___

slides.title: Nested List Comprehension
slides.prompt: What is the result of evaluating [[x for x in range(2)] for y in range(2)]?
